name: Emeka Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a ceramic tile glazing machine, checking the first tray after colour changes and calling the senior operator when the spray edge looks wrong. I joined after a delivery depot closed, so at fifty-eight I am still a junior learning this trade with secondary schooling. The wage is low for this work, and I like the first clean tray.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leena is a hospital porter, and our grown children have their own homes. We pay a housing fee, have less than a month saved and have few similar plants nearby. I use AI every day for fault notes and am curious about new controls, but I still check the tile itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tile crew that a small AI gain is still a gain if it helps us spot a glaze drift. I would keep checking the first tray myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I joined the ceramic tile plant after the delivery depot closed, so I am fifty-eight and still a junior at the glazing machine. My secondary-school certificate and daily AI log have helped me learn, but the wage is low and our reserve covers less than a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the spray heads and checking the first tiles after each colour change. I would keep using AI each day to group fault notes, and if an extra paid shift is offered, I would save a fresh portion of that wage after our housing fee and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about money, though the work itself would be familiar. Leena’s hospital-porter shifts and mine only just cover our expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you spot a bad glaze?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hold the first tile against the light and check whether the edge is dull. I still ask the senior operator before adjusting the spray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI log do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sorts my notes on blocked nozzles and colour drift. I check the shift sheet before acting, because a good sentence cannot fix a bad tile.

I would still check the **first tile** against the light.
think: My **junior wage** and thin reserve remain fragile even while the glaze machine keeps running.
Leena’s **porter shifts** and mine barely cover ordinary bills.
do: Keep **spray-head settings** and check first tiles.
Use the **existing daily AI log** for fault notes.
Save fresh **offered shift pay** after housing and food.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline bills despite familiar work.

fieldNote: Emeka’s **late career change** explains junior standing despite long work experience elsewhere.
His **daily AI use** is existing practice; new savings require an actually offered paid shift after essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to show how new ordering software changes our batch sizes before buying a faster inspection camera. A machine should earn its place on actual tiles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A camera could take the simple glaze checks I do now. I learn tools quickly, but I have the least experience on this crew; if a shift disappears, Leena’s porter pay cannot cover our housing fee alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for an offered paid guarded trial on twenty sample tiles, then learn the new AI camera’s reject settings if the supervisor approves safe practice. I would record false rejects beside my hand checks; if my hours fall, I would apply for posted reachable tile or packaging work only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own rota, but I would rather test the samples than guess. I can learn a camera menu faster than I can replace a lost pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would supervise the camera trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior operator would stop the belt and check the reject gate with me. I would need an actual paid place, not permission to watch from the aisle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there other tile plants nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very few. I would check the job board and bus fare before telling Leena that a larger headline wage solves anything.

I would ask for **paid guarded learning** on the line.
think: A camera may remove **my simple glaze checks** before I have mastered the whole line.
Leena’s **porter pay** cannot cover our housing fee alone.
do: Request **twenty-tile guarded trial** only if paid place offered.
Learn **new AI reject settings** under an approved senior operator.
Apply after **hour cuts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible loss of paid shifts.

fieldNote: His **adaptive style** makes a new camera skill plausible once an actual guarded paid place opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the glazing crew that thinking AGI could arrive by 2028 when I am sixty, while capable hands-on robots reach tiles around 2031 when I am sixty-three. The office changes first, then tile handling does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to remove most junior glaze shifts once robots can spray and inspect without us. Less than a month saved and Leena’s porter wage cannot pay our housing fee through a long loss; I would be awake at night doing the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel our planned visit to my grown son and ask the plant for written staffing dates. If my paid shifts end, I would apply for posted reachable work only if net pay after travel covers our bills; if no adequate opening appears, I would ask the housing office about temporary payment terms and our son about a pickup if he has time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the likely loss of most of my pay. I am willing to learn, but a lesson cannot create a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son pay the housing fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He has his own household and work. I would ask him for a ride to an interview if he is free, not a standing payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need actual retirement figures and Leena’s confirmed wages to cover housing and food. We do not have that assurance now.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 tile robots.
I would demand **written staffing dates** before a crew cut.
think: I expect **most junior shifts** to go with capable robots.
Our **sub-month reserve** and porter wage cannot bridge a long gap.
do: Cancel **family visit** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **housing office** about temporary terms if no job appears; ask my son only for an interview ride if free.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless housing worry.
S2.quote: I am willing to learn, but a lesson cannot create a vacancy.
fieldNote: His **age sixty-three** at physical robot arrival does not itself fund retirement.
Job and support paths retain **real conditions**: an actual vacancy, adequate net pay, housing-office approval and his son’s available time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three and capable robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years is enough to learn a new part of the plant if the job is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could work on quality sampling because I know the glaze faults, but I am still learning the records. Our low wages cannot carry unpaid classes, and a certificate is only useful if a nearby plant posts a paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the glazing shift and put a fresh amount from full paid months into our reserve. If the plant offers me a funded quality-sampling course on paid time, a safe stopped-belt practice slot and a posted reachable quality role at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying, I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years gives me a chance to see a real offer. I want to learn on a stopped belt and then be paid to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would teach sampling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A senior quality operator would show me how to measure glaze thickness and record a rejected tray. I need an offered paid place with the belt stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no quality post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid glazing shift and check actual nearby postings if hours fall. I would not buy an evening certificate for an empty board.

I would name **posted jobs** before signing up.
think: My **low wages** cannot pay for missed shifts while our housing fee keeps coming due.
A **quality certificate** helps only with adequate local work.
do: Keep **glazing shifts** and save fresh full-month surplus.

Apply after **qualification** for the reachable quality role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check an actual offer.
S3.quote: I want to learn on a stopped belt and then be paid to use it.
fieldNote: He approaches **new quality work** early but requires paid safe practice.
The later application needs **offered funded training**, a posted reachable vacancy and net wages sufficient for household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable tile robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. A decade lets us check what work and retirement can actually pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children will still have their own households. I hope to stop full-time work before seventy-one, but with less than a month saved today I cannot promise a pension or a date that covers our housing fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the glaze machine running and save fresh full-month wages after bills. I would get retirement figures with Leena; in the first year after 2036, if I am still employed because the figures require wages, I would compare real rosters and posted jobs, then apply after sustained cuts only for safe reachable work with bill-covering net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about this year’s money even with the longer horizon. A retirement estimate that cannot pay rent is just another piece of paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course at sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I still need a wage and an employer offers funded paid safe practice for a posted role, I would consider it. I would not enrol without an actual place and pay that fits our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whether they can help with a trip to an interview if schedules allow. I would not make their wages part of our retirement plan.

I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 physical tile work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable tile robots around 2031 could remove junior glaze shifts while I still need housing money. Written staffing dates, funded paid safe practice and posted reachable jobs at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a new worker my age has to show at the end of a course. I can learn quickly, but I need a paid place where the new skill is used.

headlineQuote: I can learn quickly, but I need a paid place where the new skill is used.
portrait: **Emeka**, 58, is a junior tile-glazing operator after a late move from depot work, with secondary school education and developing machine skill.
His **porter partner**, grown children, low wage, housing fee, sub-month reserve and few local plants make wage loss urgent.
He uses **AI daily** for logs and learns new camera controls only in offered paid guarded trials.
Fast robots threaten **glaze shifts** at sixty-three; longer warning permits funded quality training and an income-based retirement review.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could remove junior glazing shifts around 2031 before his household can afford to stop work.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe practice and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
